Leaderboards built from pairwise comparisons, such as Chatbot Arena, publish Bradley--Terry scores with bootstrap confidence intervals. An interval says how far the ranking moves under resampling, not how many of the existing comparisons a conclusion such as ``model $a$ is above model $b$'' rests on, or whether that number is large for such data. We measure the smallest number of comparisons whose deletion, or whose outcome change, reverses a conclusion (a verified upper bound), express it in standard-error units, and compare it with the same quantity on data simulated from the dataset's own fitted model. On crowd votes, expert labels, LLM-judge labels of the same battles and basketball seasons, the real count lies within a margin fixed in advance of that reference wherever there are enough pairs to decide; outcome flips on Arena are within the margin but not on it. Random noise of the size of the smallest adversarial change essentially never reverses a conclusion, yet separated confidence intervals do not survive small targeted changes. Matched comparisons of crowd, expert and model-judge labels on identical items show counts within the margin, though we did not test whether it detects misfit. A regression on separation, size, density and ties predicts the count for held-out datasets about as well as simulation does, and worse for a held-out design. Design is confounded with dataset, so claims concern the instances studied.
----
\paragraph{Findings.} (a) \nEquiv{} of the \nDeltaRows{} (dataset, family) rows are equivalent to the reference within the margin; the largest departure is Arena outcome flips, within the margin but not zero (Section~\ref{sec:headline}); \nInconc{} rows are undecided for want of pairs (\incList). (b) A pair separated by its confidence intervals is not robust to a targeted change of a few tenths of a percent to about one percent of the votes in the large crowd and judge datasets, and is robust to noise of the same size and to far more (Section~\ref{sec:survival}); the top place of Arena is not separated at all. (c) Judge labels on the same battles as the crowd, and GPT-4 on the same questions as the experts, show the count per unit gap within the margin of the same-graph reference in these instances, and whether the measure would detect misfit was not tested; the one design effect found is in the published interval, which for MT-Bench expert labels is about \seRatioExpert{} times the model-based one (Section~\ref{sec:design}); design is confounded with dataset, which limits what any of this says about crowds or experts in general. (d) The regression predicts $k^{*}$ for held-out datasets within a factor of about \refFBaseDel{}, no better than the dataset's own same-graph simulation, and for flips a bias-corrected first-order prediction does better; it is worse for held-out designs (Section~\ref{sec:rule}). (e) One-shot influence ranking, the usual approximation, finds the smallest change in only part of the conclusions (Section~\ref{sec:search}). Section~\ref{sec:discussion} states what the data cannot say; the code and the analysis plan are described in Appendix~\ref{app:repro}.
----
A leaderboard can report, beside the confidence interval, the number of comparisons that carry a published conclusion in standard-error units, the same number for a Bradley--Terry dataset of the same graph, and the share of separated pairs that survive a stated budget; a count far below the reference would be a misfit worth examining, though the power of this measure to show one was not tested. The same numbers could inform someone who wants to manipulate a ranking; we study no attack on a deployed platform and see the measurement as an audit.

The paper on `dev` and `candidate-v1` now reports the positive control. The wording "detection power was not tested" is replaced throughout. Still open: the Arena control cells, re-reviews of the changes, and the pull requests into `release` and `final`.

**What the control shows.** Δ stayed within ±0.15 at every size tried (34 MT-Bench cells, largest |Δ| 0.041), so it is not a test of misfit. The ratio of bootstrap to model-based standard error did respond, from 0.82 with no departure to 2.26 under the largest overdispersion. The new Appendix C and its table cover MT-Bench only.

**Arena flip Δ.** The Arena flip Δ of 0.056 is now described as mostly an offset of the method. The no-departure Arena control gives 0.045 [0.036, 0.054] from 5 replicates, and that is the only Arena control cell I quote.

**Build.** The abstract is 228 words. In a scratch build the main text ends on page 9, with no Type 3 fonts. The margin is about one line. The system build of `dev` has not been checked yet.

**Waiting on:**
- `experiment-repo`: I asked it to confirm what the quoted control numbers mean, and my description of how each departure is simulated, which I wrote from its script. I'll add the Arena rows when it says the cells are complete.
- `experiment-repo` and `figtab-repo`: I asked for re-reviews of the changed text on PR #10.

I also updated `paper-repo`#7 on the first-order rescaling constant, which is now described as fitted on the other datasets.
